# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Partner], Brukaisk Solar Holdings, LLC deal team
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 17, 2026
**Re:** Brukaisk / Rebous Rooftop Energy asset purchase: pre-Closing issues review

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

1. Executed Asset Purchase Agreement dated August 21, 2026 (APA)
2. Key Employee Agreement with Tobias Renfeld (KEA)
3. Side Letter dated August 21, 2026
4. Agreed-form Transition Services Agreement (TSA)
5. Seller Disclosure Schedule
6. July 24, 2026 draft APA
7. Buyer board consent
8. Agreed-form Bill of Sale
9. Agreed-form Indemnity Escrow Agreement

**Status of the documents.** The APA, Side Letter, Disclosure Schedule and KEA were signed or delivered on August 21, 2026. Closing is still pending, with a December 31, 2026 outside date under APA §8.1(b). The TSA, Escrow Agreement and Bill of Sale are agreed forms that will be signed at Closing.

**What that means for the fixes.**
* Fixes to the APA, Side Letter and KEA require written amendments signed by both parties (APA §11.4; Side Letter ¶5.2; KEA §10.5).
* Fixes to the TSA can be made to the form before it is signed.
* Brukaisk's main leverage is Closing itself and the still-unsigned TSA.
* These fixes should be negotiated and papered **before Closing**.

**Key economic terms for context.**

| Term | Amount | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase Price | $38,500,000 | APA §2.5 |
| General indemnity cap for rep breaches under §9.2(a) | 15% of the Purchase Price ($5,775,000) | APA §9.5(a) |
| Basket (a tipping basket, so recovery is from the first dollar once exceeded) | $385,000 | APA §9.5(b) |
| Indemnity Escrow Amount | $3,850,000, released 18 months after Closing | APA §§2.6, 9.6 |
| General survival period for representations | 18 months after the Closing Date | APA §9.1 |
| Governing law | Delaware | APA §11.8 |

I found **five issues**, ranked below by severity. Three only appear when two documents are read together.

| Rank | Issue | Location | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Side Letter moves the DOL installer-misclassification exposure from the uncapped Excluded Liabilities indemnity into the capped rep bucket | Side Letter ¶2; APA §§2.4(d), 9.2(c), 9.5(c), 11.10 | **Critical** |
| 2 | Installed-systems (workmanship) representations survive only 90 days | APA §9.1(b); Disclosure Schedule 4.9, Part A | **Critical** |
| 3 | Renfeld's non-compete and non-solicit cover only residential solar installation | KEA §§1.1, 7.1; APA §1.1 | **High** |
| 4 | Buyer gives Seller an uncapped indemnity that covers Seller's own negligence | TSA §§7.1, 7.2, 8.2, 8.3 | **High** |
| 5 | Seller may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone without Buyer's consent | TSA §12.3 | **Medium-High** |

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1 (Critical): Side Letter caps the installer misclassification liability

**Where:**
* Side Letter, Paragraph 2.
* Read with APA §§2.4(d), 9.2(a), 9.2(c), 9.5(a)–(c), 9.1 and 11.10.
* Disclosure Schedule 4.13(c), item 1.

**What it says.**

The APA, standing alone, protects Brukaisk fully:
* §2.4(d) makes Excluded Liabilities include all liabilities from Seller's pre-Closing employment or engagement of individuals. This expressly covers "any classification of any individual as an independent contractor rather than an employee."
* §9.2(c) indemnifies Buyer for Excluded Liabilities.
* §9.5(c) provides that the 15% cap and the Basket "shall not apply to claims under Section 9.2(b) or Section 9.2(c)." Those claims are limited only by the Purchase Price backstop.
* §9.1's survival periods apply to representations, not to the §9.2(c) indemnity. §9.4's pre-expiry notice requirement applies only to §9.2(a) claims.

The Side Letter changes this:
* It defines the "Installer Classification Matter" as the May 2026 U.S. Department of Labor Wage and Hour audit of Seller's engagement of installers, electricians and crew leads as independent contractors since January 1, 2023. It includes related or successor proceedings and individual claims.
* Paragraph 2 provides that Losses from that matter are recoverable "**solely as Losses arising from a breach** of the representations and warranties of Seller in Section 4.13(c)," whether or not disclosed.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk.**
* Read alone, ¶2 looks Buyer-friendly, because Seller's disclosure in Schedule 4.13(c) cannot defeat the claim. Its real effect is the opposite.
* Section 4.13(c) is **not** a Fundamental Representation. The Fundamental Representations are §§4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.14 and 4.16 only. A §4.13(c) claim is therefore a §9.2(a) claim, subject to:
  * the **15% cap** ($5,775,000), shared with every other rep claim, including the workmanship claims in Issue 2;
  * the **$385,000 Basket**; and
  * the **18-month survival** period with the §9.4 pre-expiry notice requirement.
* The word "solely" removes the §9.2(c) route.
* Under APA §11.10, the Side Letter **ranks first** in the order of precedence between Buyer and Seller. It controls over APA §§2.4(d) and 9.5(c).
* The July 24 draft had no precedence clause; its §11.10 was specific performance. The precedence ranking was added between draft and signing, which makes the shift harder to argue away.

**Size of the exposure.**
* Schedule 4.13(c) discloses 137 independent-contractor installers engaged since January 1, 2023.
* The audit covers back wages, overtime and recordkeeping under the FLSA. Liquidated damages can double back-wage awards.
* Related payroll-tax, state wage-law and private claims are plausible.
* This is the single known, quantifiable liability in the deal. It is exactly the kind of risk the uncapped Excluded Liabilities indemnity was meant to cover.
* Under the Side Letter, it competes for the same capped pool as every other rep claim.
* Agency or successor proceedings can outlast 18 months. A noticed claim survives under §9.4, but any later-arising claims could be time-barred.
* There is also a practical risk. DOL and private plaintiffs may pursue Brukaisk as a successor employer if it engages the same crews (see Side Letter ¶4). That makes a full, uncapped indemnity from Seller essential.

**Recommended fix.** Amend the Side Letter (¶5.2 requires a writing signed by both parties) so that Losses from the Installer Classification Matter:
* are recoverable under APA §9.2(c) as Excluded Liabilities, and, at Buyer's election, also under §9.2(a);
* are expressly **not subject** to the §9.5(a) cap, the §9.5(b) Basket, or the §9.1 survival periods and §9.4 notice deadline; and
* expressly "shall not reduce or count against" the 15% cap available for other claims.

Also consider the following, given that the matter is known and still open:
* a special escrow or holdback sized to a reasonable estimate of the audit exposure, with release tied to final resolution of the matter rather than the 18-month date;
* Buyer control of, or consent rights over, the defense and settlement after Closing, beyond the limited consent right in Side Letter ¶3.2; and
* a conforming change to the Escrow Agreement if a special escrow is used.

**Board authority.** The board consent (§7) bars officers from approving Side Letter amendments that change the Purchase Price or Indemnity Escrow Amount without further Board approval. A pure restoration of §9.2(c) treatment does not trigger that requirement. A new special escrow carved out of the Purchase Price may, so confirm Board sign-off before agreeing one.

---

### Issue 2 (Critical): Installed-systems representations die 90 days after Closing

**Where:**
* APA §9.1, proviso (b).
* APA §1.1, definition of "Specified Warranty Period."
* Disclosure Schedule 4.9, Part A.

**What it says.**
* APA §9.1 sets general survival at **18 months after the Closing Date**.
* It then provides that the §4.9 representations (Installed Systems) "shall survive **until the expiration of the Specified Warranty Period**." These cover:
  * good and workmanlike installation;
  * code, permit and interconnection compliance; and
  * no roof-penetration, flashing, leak, water-intrusion or structural defects.
* APA §1.1 says that term "has the meaning given in Schedule 4.9."
* Schedule 4.9, Part A defines it as the period "beginning on the Closing Date and **ending ninety (90) days after the Closing Date**." That is the window during which Seller keeps administering pre-Closing warranty claims.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk.**
* Read alone, §9.1(b) looks like an *extended* survival tied to the long customer warranties. Read with the Schedule, the workmanship and leak representations expire **90 days after Closing**. That is far shorter than the 18-month general period.
* §9.4 bars any §9.2(a) claim unless notice is given before the survival period ends.
* §9.1 states that the survival periods replace the statute of limitations. Delaware enforces contractually shortened survival periods (see 10 Del. C. § 8106(c) and related case law).
* Latent installation defects surface years later, not within 90 days. Roof leaks, flashing failures, racking and structural problems, and code non-compliance found on later inspection all fall in this category. The Schedule confirms the scale:
  * 6,842 residential contracts carrying 10-year roof-penetration warranties and 10- to 25-year workmanship warranties;
  * 54 commercial EPC contracts with 10-year workmanship warranties;
  * 71 confirmed installation-caused leaks repaired at $286,400 in 2023–2026;
  * an open commercial water-intrusion claim of about $46,000;
  * 23 systems lacking final inspection sign-off; and
  * an incomplete racking-recall retrofit on 18 systems.
* Brukaisk takes the Customer Contracts and will face customer warranty demands. Assumed Liabilities under §2.3(b) exclude pre-Closing warranty breaches. In practice, though, Brukaisk will have to repair to protect customer relationships and the brand.
* After day 90, Brukaisk would have no rep-based recourse. It would have to argue that each defect is a pre-Closing Excluded Liability under §2.4(a) or §2.3(b). Seller will contest that, and the specific survival language in §9.1(b) will be cited against it.
* The July 24 draft §9.1 contained no §4.9 proviso. This carve-out entered the deal at signing.

**Recommended fix.** Amend APA §9.1(b) so §4.9 survival is a **stated period in the APA itself, independent of any Schedule definition**.
* At minimum, the period should be no shorter than the general 18-month survival.
* Preferably, it should run until the expiration of the longest applicable customer workmanship or roof-penetration warranty (10 years for roof penetration), or a negotiated fixed period such as 5–7 years.
* Delete the cross-reference to "Specified Warranty Period" in §9.1. If the term is still needed for Seller's warranty-administration role, keep it only in that context.
* Expressly confirm that Buyer may recover installation-defect Losses under §9.2(c) as Excluded Liabilities, in addition to §9.2(a).
* Consider removing §4.9 claims from the shared 15% cap, or giving them their own sub-cap.
* Consider extending the escrow, or creating a warranty holdback, beyond the 18-month release.

---

### Issue 3 (High): Founder non-compete does not cover most of the acquired Business

**Where:**
* KEA §1.1 ("Business") and §7.1.
* Compare APA §1.1 ("Business") and APA §6.6.

**What it says.**
* APA §1.1 defines the Business Brukaisk is buying as "the design, sale, installation, maintenance and monitoring of **residential and commercial solar energy and battery storage systems**."
* KEA §1.1 defines "Business" as "the **installation of residential solar photovoltaic systems**."
* KEA §7.1 binds Renfeld only with respect to "the Business" as the KEA defines it. That covers:
  * the non-compete in §7.1(a);
  * customer non-solicit in §7.1(b);
  * employee and installer non-solicit in §7.1(c); and
  * supplier non-interference in §7.1(d).

**Why it matters to Brukaisk.**
* The KEA is between Brukaisk and Renfeld personally. APA §11.10's precedence clause applies only "as between Buyer and Seller." It does not import the APA definition into the KEA.
* Renfeld could, immediately after Closing (or immediately after leaving), compete or solicit in any of the following without breaching the KEA:
  * commercial solar, including the 54 commercial EPC and 29 O&M customers;
  * battery storage;
  * maintenance and O&M;
  * monitoring, which is the Monitoring Platform business;
  * design and sales.
* The employee non-solicit in §7.1(c) is also limited to personnel engaged "in the Business." Renfeld could recruit Brukaisk's commercial, storage, service and monitoring staff.
* The APA §6.6 non-compete binds only Seller and its Affiliates. Whether Renfeld, as majority shareholder, counts as an "Affiliate" is arguable. Relying on that is weak, and the specific KEA covenant will be read as the agreed scope of his personal restriction.
* The KEA recitals say the covenants are a material inducement to the deal. KEA §7.3(b) frames them as sale-of-business covenants, which Delaware reviews more leniently. The narrow definition wastes that.
* Brukaisk is paying $38.5 million largely for goodwill and customer relationships across all of these lines. A court applying KEA §7.5 reformation will narrow an overbroad covenant, but it will not expand a narrow one.

**Recommended fix.**
* Amend KEA §1.1 so "Business" has the meaning given in APA §1.1. Better, restate it in full and add "and any business competitive with any of the foregoing."
* Make conforming changes to the "Customer" definition and to §7.1(a)–(d).
* Because the KEA is effective at Closing and is a Buyer closing condition under APA §7.2(e), obtain the amendment as a signed KEA amendment **delivered at or before Closing**.
* Consider also obtaining a direct seller-level restrictive covenant from Renfeld as shareholder, mirroring APA §6.6.

---

### Issue 4 (High): Uncapped Buyer indemnity covering Seller's own negligence under the TSA

**Where:** TSA §§7.1, 7.2, 8.2 and 8.3.

**What it says.**
* **TSA §7.1:** Recipient (Brukaisk) must indemnify Provider (Seller) for "any and all Losses arising out of or relating to the Services," "**including Losses arising from Provider's negligence** in performing the Services." The only carve-out is Provider's gross negligence or willful misconduct.
* **TSA §7.2:** Provider's indemnity of Recipient covers only Provider's *gross* negligence or willful misconduct.
* **TSA §8.2:** Each party's liability is capped at Service Fees paid.
* **TSA §8.3:** The cap "**shall not apply to Recipient's obligations under Section 7.1**."

**Why it matters to Brukaisk.**
* Delaware enforces indemnities covering the indemnitee's own negligence when the language is clear and unequivocal. Here it is express.
* The result is a one-way allocation:
  * Brukaisk bears **unlimited** liability for Seller's ordinary negligence.
  * Seller's exposure to Brukaisk is narrow (gross negligence or willful misconduct only) and capped at fees.
* Fees run roughly $109,000 per month across Services A-1 to A-5, so the cap on Seller is roughly $650,000 for the 6-month term.
* The services carry real third-party risk:
  * **Monitoring Platform hosting (A-1):** a negligent data breach exposes customer personal and payment data.
  * **Permitting and interconnection (A-2):** negligent filings risk code violations, fines and fire-safety claims.
  * **Call center (A-3):** misrouted warranty and safety calls.
  * **Billing (A-4).**
* If Seller's staff negligently cause a breach or a faulty permit, Brukaisk would have to indemnify Seller for the resulting customer and regulatory claims, without limit.
* This also undercuts TSA §5.3 (Provider's security obligations) and the Service Standard in §3.1.

**Recommended fix.** Revise the TSA form before signing at Closing:
* Limit §7.1 to Losses arising from Recipient's own negligence, willful misconduct or breach, and Recipient's operation of the Business after Closing.
* Delete "including Losses arising from Provider's negligence."
* Expressly exclude Losses caused by Provider's negligence, breach of the Service Standard, breach of §5 (data) or §6 (confidentiality), or violation of Law.
* Make §7.2 reciprocal, so Provider indemnifies for its negligence, breach and data incidents.
* Delete the §7.1 exception in §8.3, so any Buyer indemnity falls under the §8.2 cap.
* If any carve-outs from the cap remain, make them mutual. Examples: data-security breaches, confidentiality, and willful misconduct, applied to Provider as well.

---

### Issue 5 (Medium-High): Seller may assign or delegate the TSA to anyone, including a competitor

**Where:** TSA §12.3. Compare APA §11.6 and Escrow Agreement §10.4.

**What it says.**
* TSA §12.3 lets Provider assign the TSA, or "delegate the performance of any of the Services, to any Person **without the consent of Recipient**."
* Recipient may not assign without Provider's consent.
* APA §11.6 restricts assignment of the APA only. It does not reach the TSA.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk.**
* During the 6-month term, Seller could hand the services to a competing installer or an unvetted vendor. Those services include:
  * running the Monitoring Platform, which holds all of Brukaisk's newly acquired Customer Data;
  * staffing the call center that speaks to Brukaisk's customers "in the name of the Business"; and
  * handling permitting and billing.
* That gives a third party direct access to the customer base Brukaisk just paid for. Confidentiality and data-use protections in TSA §§5–6 would be enforceable only against Seller, and only up to the capped and narrowed remedies discussed in Issue 4.
* The one-sidedness also prevents Brukaisk from assigning the TSA to an Affiliate or acquisition-financing lender. That is inconsistent with its rights under APA §11.6.

**Recommended fix.** Revise TSA §12.3:
* Make it mutual. Neither party may assign or delegate without the other's prior written consent.
* Allow Recipient to assign without consent to Affiliates, lenders (as collateral) and successors, mirroring APA §11.6.
* Prohibit any assignment or delegation by Provider to a competitor of the Business.
* Require any permitted subcontractor to be bound in writing by the data, security and confidentiality terms in §§5–6.
* Keep Provider fully liable for its subcontractors.
* Provide that a non-compliant assignment is void.

---

## III. Documents reviewed with no additional issues

* **July 24, 2026 draft APA.** This is superseded and has no operative effect. It is useful for comparison only. It lacked both the §9.1(b) Specified Warranty Period proviso (Issue 2) and the §11.10 precedence clause that elevates the Side Letter (Issue 1). Both protections were lost between Buyer's draft and the signed agreement, which is a useful negotiating point.
* **Buyer board consent.** It approves the "substantially final" Transaction Documents and authorizes officers to approve changes. Officers may not approve amendments to the APA or Side Letter that change the Purchase Price or Indemnity Escrow Amount without further Board approval. The fixes above do not require Board action unless a special escrow or holdback is created from the Purchase Price (Issue 1). I nonetheless recommend briefing the Board on these items before Closing.
* **Bill of Sale (form).** No issues. §6 confirms non-merger of the APA representations and indemnities.
* **Indemnity Escrow Agreement (form).** No issues on its own terms. The escrow ($3.85 million) releases 18 months after Closing. Conforming changes may be needed if a special misclassification escrow or extended warranty holdback is agreed (Issues 1 and 2).

---

## IV. Recommended next steps

1. Prepare a short APA and Side Letter amendment addressing Issues 1 and 2, and a KEA amendment addressing Issue 3. Seek signature before Closing.
2. Mark up the TSA form for Issues 4 and 5. It has not yet been signed and is a Closing deliverable under APA §§3.2(c) and 3.3(c).
3. Treat the amendments as a practical condition to Brukaisk proceeding to Closing, keeping the December 31, 2026 outside date in view.
4. Obtain a current status update and exposure estimate on the DOL audit (Side Letter ¶3.1) to size any special escrow.

Please let me know if you would like draft amendment language for any of these items.

**Date:** November 17, 2026
**Re:** Brukaisk Solar Holdings, LLC / Rebous Rooftop Energy, Inc. – Issues in the Transaction Documents

## I. Summary

We act for Brukaisk Solar Holdings, LLC ("**Buyer**" or "**Brukaisk**") in its purchase of substantially all of the assets of Rebous Rooftop Energy, Inc. ("**Seller**"). The deal terms are:

## II. Issues

### Issue 1 – Side Letter Caps the Known Installer Misclassification Exposure (CRITICAL)

**Location:**
- Side Letter, Paragraph 2.
- Read with APA Sections 2.4(d), 9.2(a), 9.2(c), 9.5(a)–(c), 9.1 and 11.10.

**What the documents say:**

1. *The APA alone.* Liabilities from Seller's pre-Closing engagement of individuals are Excluded Liabilities under APA § 2.4(d). That expressly includes "any classification of any individual as an independent contractor rather than an employee." Buyer is indemnified for Excluded Liabilities under § 9.2(c). Under § 9.5(c), the 15% cap and the $385,000 Basket "shall not apply to claims under Section 9.2(b) or Section 9.2(c)." On the APA alone, the misclassification exposure is therefore uncapped (subject only to the Purchase Price ceiling). It is also outside the Basket and not tied to the representation survival period.

2. *The Side Letter.* Paragraph 2 provides that Losses from the "Installer Classification Matter" are recoverable "solely as Losses arising from a breach of the representations and warranties of Seller in Section 4.13(c)." The defined term covers:
   - the May 2026 U.S. Department of Labor Wage and Hour Division audit;
   - any successor proceeding; and
   - individual claims arising from the same facts.

   The paragraph adds that disclosure does not qualify § 4.13(c). This looks protective on its face.

3. *The combined effect.* Section 4.13(c) is not a Fundamental Representation (APA § 1.1). A claim under it is therefore a § 9.2(a) claim, and as a result it is:
   - subject to the 15% cap of $5,775,000 (§ 9.5(a));
   - subject to the $385,000 Basket (§ 9.5(b)); and
   - limited to the general survival period of 18 months after the Closing Date (§ 9.1), with notice required before expiry (§ 9.4).

4. *Precedence.* Under APA § 11.10, the Side Letter ranks first, ahead of the APA. The word "solely" therefore displaces the § 9.2(c) route.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk:**

- This is a known and quantifiable risk. Disclosure Schedule 4.13(c) reports 137 individuals engaged as independent contractors since January 1, 2023.
- The audit covers wages, overtime and recordkeeping, and no findings have yet been issued.
- Back wages, liquidated damages under the FLSA, penalties and parallel state-law and private claims could be large and could arise over a long period.
- If Brukaisk hires these installers or continues the business with the same workforce, it also faces successor-liability arguments.
- Under the Side Letter as drafted:
  - the misclassification exposure shares the same $5,775,000 cap as every other representation claim;
  - the first $385,000 of aggregate § 9.2(a) Losses must accrue before Seller pays anything; and
  - any claim not noticed within 18 months is lost, even though DOL and private claims could be asserted later.
- The board consent (D7, ¶7) also limits officer authority over amendments to the Side Letter only where they change price or escrow. Signing off on this conversion did not need board escalation, which may explain why it was missed.

**Recommended fix:** Amend Paragraph 2 of the Side Letter so that Losses from the Installer Classification Matter are recoverable **under Section 9.2(c) as Excluded Liabilities**. The amendment should provide that:

- this recovery is in addition to, and not in substitution for, any claim under § 9.2(a);
- §§ 9.5(a) and 9.5(b) do not apply; and
- the claim survives until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations or the final resolution of the matter, whichever is later.

Delete "solely." Keep the sentence stating that disclosure does not qualify § 4.13(c). Also consider:

- a specific escrow holdback, or an increase in the Indemnity Escrow, sized to a reasonable estimate of the DOL exposure and released only when the matter is resolved; and
- Buyer control of, or consent rights over, post-Closing conduct and settlement.

---

### Issue 2 – Uncapped Buyer Indemnity of Seller, Including for Seller's Own Negligence (HIGH)

**Location:** TSA (agreed form), Sections 7.1, 7.2, 8.2 and 8.3.

**What the documents say:**

- **§ 7.1:** Brukaisk, as Recipient, must indemnify Seller, as Provider, against "any and all Losses arising out of or relating to the Services ... including Losses arising from Provider's negligence in performing the Services." The only carve-out is Provider's gross negligence or willful misconduct.
- **§ 7.2:** Seller's reciprocal indemnity covers only its own gross negligence or willful misconduct.
- **§ 8.2:** Each party's liability is capped at total Service Fees paid. Schedule A fees total roughly $109,000 per month, so the cap is well under $700,000 over the 6-month Term.
- **§ 8.3:** The cap "shall not apply to Recipient's obligations under Section 7.1."
- **§ 8.1:** The consequential damages exclusion carves out amounts paid to third parties under a § 7 indemnity.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk:**

- Delaware enforces indemnities for the indemnitee's own negligence where the language is clear and unequivocal. Section 7.1 states it expressly, so a court is likely to enforce it as written.
- Brukaisk therefore bears unlimited liability for Seller's ordinary negligence in delivering the services, while Seller's liability to Brukaisk is narrow and capped. The services carry real risk:
  - **Monitoring Platform hosting (A-1):** data breaches involving Customer Data, and missed system alerts.
  - **Permitting and interconnection (A-2):** code-compliance failures and missed filings on active jobs.
  - **Call center (A-3):** mishandled warranty and safety calls.
- If Seller negligently lets a breach of customer data occur, Brukaisk would bear Seller's own losses for that breach on top of its own.
- This inverts the normal TSA allocation, under which the provider bears the risk of its own performance failures.

**Recommended fix:**

- Revise § 7.1 so Recipient indemnifies only for Losses arising from Recipient's own negligence, willful misconduct or breach, or from its operation of the Business after Closing. Delete the express reference to Provider's negligence, and exclude any Losses to the extent caused by Provider.
- Make § 7.2 mutual, so that Provider indemnifies for its negligence and its breach of the Service Standard, Section 5 (data security) and Section 6 (confidentiality).
- Delete the § 7.1 exception in § 8.3, so that Recipient's indemnity falls under the § 8.2 cap.
- Add uncapped carve-outs from § 8.2 for Provider's data security and confidentiality breaches and its gross negligence or willful misconduct.

---

### Issue 3 – Founder Non-Compete Uses a Narrower Definition of "Business" (HIGH)

**Location:**
- Key Employee Agreement, Sections 1.1 ("Business") and 7.1.
- Compare APA Section 1.1 ("Business").

**What the documents say:**

- **APA § 1.1:** The Business Brukaisk is buying is "the design, sale, installation, maintenance and monitoring of residential and commercial solar energy and battery storage systems."
- **KEA § 1.1:** "Business" means only "the installation of residential solar photovoltaic systems."
- **KEA § 7.1:** Every one of Renfeld's restrictive covenants is keyed to "the Business" as the KEA defines it:
  - (a) the non-compete;
  - (b) the customer non-solicit;
  - (c) the employee and installer non-solicit; and
  - (d) the non-interference covenant.
- The KEA's "Customer" definition is keyed to the same narrow term.
- The KEA is between Buyer and Renfeld individually. APA § 11.10 governs precedence only "as between Buyer and Seller." It does not import the APA definition into the KEA.
- The Seller-level non-compete in APA § 6.6 uses the broader definition, but it binds Seller and its Affiliates, not necessarily Renfeld acting through a new vehicle.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk:**

- Recital D of the KEA records that Renfeld's covenants are a material inducement to the purchase. Yet he could compete on the day after Closing in:
  - commercial solar, including the 54 commercial EPC and 29 commercial O&M contracts (Schedule 4.8, Part B);
  - battery storage;
  - design and sales;
  - maintenance; and
  - monitoring, which is the core of the Monitoring Platform and the RMS-2021 subscription base.
- He could also solicit commercial and storage customers, and the 22 service and 24 monitoring and support employees, in those lines.
- Renfeld is the person with the most knowledge of, and the strongest relationships in, the business. That puts at risk the goodwill Brukaisk is paying for.
- A Delaware court may decline to "blue pencil" the covenant wider. The § 7.5 reformation clause only narrows a covenant to make it enforceable.

**Recommended fix:** Amend KEA § 1.1 to define "Business" by express cross-reference to the APA definition: "the design, sale, installation, maintenance and monitoring of residential and commercial solar energy and battery storage systems," as conducted by Seller as of the APA date and as conducted by the Company during the Term.

Make sure the "Customer" definition and all four limbs of § 7.1 pick up the broader term. Because the KEA is already signed, the amendment needs Renfeld's signature. It should be a condition to Closing, alongside the existing condition in APA § 7.2(e). The covenant remains reasonable in the sale-of-business context because Renfeld is the majority seller.

### Issue 4 – Seller's Unrestricted Right to Assign or Delegate the TSA (MEDIUM-HIGH)

**Location:** TSA (agreed form), Section 12.3.

**What the documents say:**

- Provider "may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, or delegate the performance of any of the Services, to any Person without the consent of Recipient."
- Recipient may not assign without Provider's consent.
- APA § 11.6 restricts assignment of the APA only. It does not reach the TSA.

**Why it matters to Brukaisk:**

- Over the 6-month Term, Seller will run the Monitoring Platform, which holds Brukaisk's newly acquired Customer Data. It will also staff the call center that answers Brukaisk's customers in the name of the Business.
- Section 12.3 would let Seller hand those functions, and the Customer Data, to any third party, including a competing installer. The new provider would not have been vetted for security or quality.
- The protections in §§ 5 and 6 would bind only the assignee. Brukaisk would also lose control over who speaks to its customers during the most sensitive phase of integration.
- The one-sided consent right also restricts Brukaisk's own ability to restructure, for example by assigning the TSA to an Affiliate or to a lender.

**Recommended fix:** Make § 12.3 mutual, along these lines:

- Neither party may assign the TSA, or delegate any Service, without the other's prior written consent.
- Buyer may assign without consent to an Affiliate, a lender (as collateral) or a successor to the Business, mirroring APA § 11.6.
- No assignment or delegation is permitted to any Person that competes with the Business.
- Any permitted subcontractor must be bound by §§ 5 and 6.
- Provider remains fully liable for its delegates.
